extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in social media history and short-form video platforms
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia article describing Vine (the six‑second looping video service): its features, history, usage, reception, competitors, and successors. Focus is on platform constraints, feature set, and cultural impact rather than prescriptive guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Video length limit (six seconds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vine was a short-form video hosting service where users could share up to 6-second-long looping video clips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The platform constrained creators to very short clips (six seconds), which shaped the form and pacing of content; elsewhere the article notes videos could have lasted between two and six-and-a-half seconds in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Looping playback and loop counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Videos published on Vine were looping; Vine introduced a "loop count" showing how many times a vine was viewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loop counts included views from embedded instances on other sites; the endless looping plus visible loop metrics influenced how creators constructed repeatable, meme‑friendly content.

rubrics_metrics.name: In-app camera recording behavior (touch-to-record)
rubrics_metrics.description: The camera would record only while the screen was being touched, enabling users to edit on the fly or create stop motion effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This input constraint is also a production affordance — creators used touch-to-record for on-the-fly edits, micro-timing, and stop-motion techniques specific to six‑second content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Camera tools: grid and ghost image
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional features included grid and ghost image tools for the camera.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tools supported composition and continuity tricks (useful for animation/stop-motion and precise framing), encouraging certain production workflows for short-form clips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sharing features: "revine" and curated channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Vine added curated channels (including themed areas and trending topics/users) and the ability to "revine" (share again, similar to Twitter's 'retweet') videos on a personal stream.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curated channels and revining were distribution mechanisms that affected discoverability and virality; creators could rely on these features to reach wider audiences and participate in trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protected posts
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protected posts allowed creators to restrict visibility/audience, a platform-level privacy/control feature relevant to who can view content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music feature: Vine Music 'Snap to Beat'
rubrics_metrics.description: In August 2015, Vine introduced Vine Music, whose 'Snap to Beat' feature creates perfect infinite music loops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Snap to Beat enabled precise musical timing and looping for audio-driven content, facilitating music‑synchronized comedic or musical micro‑performances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment: longer attached clips (up to 140 seconds)
rubrics_metrics.description: In June 2016, Vine announced that it was experimenting with letting users attach video clips up to 140 seconds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was an experimental departure from the six‑second core constraint and signaled tensions between short‑form identity and longer formats; the note is descriptive rather than normative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vine Kids curation and target age
rubrics_metrics.description: Vine Kids was an app designed for children aged 7 to 12; every video posted to the app was selected by Vine employees to ensure their safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vine Kids' curated approach mandated human selection of content for child-appropriate consumption, indicating stricter editorial control and content-safety procedures compared with the main app.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content policy and age-rating response (pornography handling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vine faced criticism for how it handled pornography; porn is not forbidden by Twitter's guidelines and one sexually explicit clip was accidentally featured as an 'Editor's Pick'. Because pornography violates Apple's terms of service, the app's rating was changed to 17+ in February 2013 following a request by Apple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This highlights platform moderation and external app-store constraints: even if platform guidelines did not ban porn, third‑party store policies forced an age‑rating change and affected perceived suitability of the app.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary content uses and genres
rubrics_metrics.description: Vine attracted different types of uses, including short-form comedy and music performances, video editing, and stop motion animation; it was also used for news documentation and promotional/marketing uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists common and successful use cases (comedy, music, stop-motion, promotional campaigns, news) which function as descriptive guidance about formats and genres that perform well on a six‑second looping platform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform archival and successor considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter launched an online archive of every Vine video; successors (Byte/Clash/Huddles, DiVine) have sought to replicate the six‑second looping format and/or restore archived Vines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archivability and successor design choices (length, looping, content migration/DMCA handling, AI detection for synthetic content) are platform-level standards that impact how creators think about long-term availability and reuse of their work.
